clue.text: A club to set up church teaching? Proper shambles

parts.note: a bat is a club for hitting a ball

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting something up raises it, so these letters read bottom to top

parts.note: RI is religious instruction, the school subject

explanation.surface: A sports club arranging Sunday school lessons turns out to be a complete mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' turns RI into IR at the foot of the entry. 'Proper' says shambles is meant in its original, literal sense rather than 'a mess'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shambles was originally a meat market or slaughterhouse, which is exactly what an abattoir is.

clue.text: Tees had turned old instrument tone down

indicators.note: turned round, so the letters of the short form are read backwards

parts.note: the setter, Tees, says 'I had', shortened to I'D
the lute is an old plucked string instrument

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to having softened the sound of an antique instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' makes I'D into DI. A setter often refers to themselves by their pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To dilute something is to weaken it, just as toning down makes it less strong.

clue.text: Modest disrobing?

definitions.meaning: playfully, ... is taking clothes off, since to assume is to put on

explanation.surface: A modest person taking their clothes off?
explanation.definitionFit: An unassuming person makes no claims for themselves, i.e. is modest; to assume a garment is to don it.

clue.text: Red route south from Leeds seen in advance

indicators.note: the motorway is seen inside the other word, so one goes within the other

parts.note: to come is to move forward, advance
the M1 motorway runs from Leeds south to London; written MI with an I for the 1

explanation.surface: A communist takes the motorway down from Leeds and arrives early.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main north–south motorway, running between Leeds and London; the digit 1 is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A Red is a communist, and commie is the informal, dismissive word for one.

clue.text: Got going? By implication no!

parts.note: read the answer as an instruction: the word on, turned round, gives the clue's word no

explanation.surface: A question about whether something started, met with a firm denial.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer, read as wordplay, makes the clue word, since ON turned gives NO. 'By implication' flags that trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who got going in the sense of being aroused or started up has been turned on.

clue.text: Son breaks mirror in domed recess

indicators.note: the abbreviation breaks into the other word, splitting it

parts.note: to ape is to copy or mirror someone

explanation.surface: A boy smashes a looking-glass hanging in a church alcove.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the vaulted semicircular recess at the end of a church, typically roofed with a half-dome.

clue.text: Philosophy old yogi developed around energy

indicators.note: the rearranged letters wrap around the symbol
developed suggests something worked into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: An elderly yogi has evolved a philosophy built on energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developed' rearranges OLD YOGI into IDEOLOGY's letters less E; 'around' puts them round E.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideology is a system of ideas and beliefs, a body of thought like a philosophy.

clue.text: Shocked at gash that looks nasty

indicators.note: a nasty-looking wound is a twisted mess, so these letters get jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone recoils at the sight of an ugly wound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that looks nasty' rearranges AT GASH.
explanation.definitionFit: To be aghast is to be filled with horror or shock.

clue.text: Very naughty boy born our bastard High King

parts.note: in Monty Python's Life of Brian, Brian's mother says he is 'a very naughty boy'

indicators.note: used as an adjective, bastard means corrupted or irregular, so these letters are spoiled into a new order

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a disreputable child born to an Irish ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bastard' rearranges OUR into ORU. Brian Boru was the eleventh-century High King of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Boru held the title Ard Rí, High King of Ireland, before dying at Clontarf in 1014.

clue.text: Schweinehund one good to be released as stray?

indicators.note: the abbreviation is let go, so it leaves the word

parts.note: German for pig-dog: Schwein is pig and Hund is dog

explanation.surface: A German insult for a cur, set free to wander the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be released' takes the first G out of PIGDOG. Schweinehund is a German term of abuse literally meaning pig-dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A pi-dog is an ownerless half-wild dog of Asian villages, essentially a stray.

clue.text: Tory woman in support for corporation?

definitions.meaning: Liz ..., Conservative politician, then Foreign Secretary
a padded belt supporting a hernia; corporation is jocular old slang for a paunch

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician backing big business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corporation' is not business here but an old British joke word for a pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Liz Truss is a Conservative; a truss is a surgical appliance holding a hernia in the abdomen.

clue.text: Mother outside hotel beginning to enter drunk state

indicators.note: the parent word sits outside the rest, wrapping it

parts.note: MA is an informal word for mother
an inn is a small hotel

indicators.note: only the first letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: a sot is a drunkard

explanation.surface: Mum waits outside the hotel as a drunk starts to come in, in a bad state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts the parent word around the rest. 'state' looks like a condition someone is in; it is one of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Minnesota is one of the United States, in the Upper Midwest.

clue.text: Old poetry university dons do to death

indicators.note: verse dons, puts on, the abbreviation like clothing, so it goes inside

parts.note: verse is poetry

explanation.surface: Academics at a university kill old poetry by over-analysing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dons' looks like university lecturers but is the verb 'puts on', placing U inside VERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something to death is to repeat it until it is stale, i.e. to overuse it.

clue.text: Non-oven-ready option: create vacancy for 11?

definitions.meaning: what you do with food that is frozen rather than ready to cook; also a nod to the 'oven-ready' Brexit deal
remove Lord Frost, the Brexit minister, whose resignation left his brief to Truss, the answer at 11

explanation.surface: A political puzzle about a Brexit deal not ready to go and a post opening up.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Frost resigned as Brexit minister in December 2021 and his role passed to Liz Truss. Boris Johnson called his Brexit deal 'oven-ready'.
explanation.definitionFit: To defrost food is to thaw it before it can be cooked; to de-Frost is to remove Frost from office.

clue.text: Huge great king around house being old man?

parts.note: fat can mean huge, as in a fat profit

indicators.note: the king's name goes around the abbreviation

parts.note: Herod the Great, king of Judea

explanation.surface: A huge, great king surrounding a house suggests a hefty patriarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great' is not an adjective beside 'huge' but part of Herod the Great's title. 'old man' is slang for father.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatherhood is the state of being a father, and old man is informal for one's father.

clue.text: Maimonides for one having no time to talk

indicators.note: the abbreviation is absent from the slang word

parts.note: to rabbit is British slang for talking on and on

explanation.surface: A medieval sage too busy to stop and chat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabbit (on)' is British slang for chattering endlessly. Maimonides was a twelfth-century Jewish scholar.
explanation.definitionFit: Maimonides was a celebrated medieval Jewish scholar and teacher, an example of a rabbi.

clue.text: Hunks crossing ring road to get port or claret

indicators.note: the hunks straddle the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: beaux are handsome men, admirers
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: Muscular men cross a ring road heading for a drink of port or red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' looks like the fortified wine but means a port city, so the definition covers the place and its wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Bordeaux is a French port on the Garonne, and claret is the British name for its red wine.

clue.text: Wrong end of torpedo going off

indicators.note: the word's final letter is the one in question
that last letter goes away from the word

parts.note: to torpedo a ship is to sink it

explanation.surface: Something has gone wrong with a torpedo's tail as it fires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going off' looks like the torpedo exploding; with 'end of' it removes the last letter of SINK.
explanation.definitionFit: A sin is a wrong, a moral offence.

clue.text: Ignore symptom Spooner reports in good weather

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the opening sounds trade places

parts.note: to shun is to ignore or avoid
a sign is a symptom of illness

explanation.surface: Advice to overlook a medical symptom during fine weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the starts of SHUN SIGN by sound gives SUN SHINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunshine is bright sunny weather, the kind generally thought good.

clue.text: Tasty plant in porridge, we hear

indicators.note: the clue tells us to listen, so the answer sounds like that slang word

parts.note: porridge is British slang for a prison sentence, i.e. time

explanation.surface: A flavoursome herb stirred into the breakfast oats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'porridge' is not oats but British slang for time in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Thyme is a herb used to flavour food, so a plant that tastes good.

clue.text: Separate book top class won't need

indicators.note: the abbreviation is dispensed with, so it leaves the word

parts.note: best can mean top, as in the top or best student
a range is a class or category of goods

explanation.surface: A top class at school doesn't need a textbook, so it is split up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'won't need' drops the B from BEST + RANGE. 'top class' looks like one phrase but supplies two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange people is to drive them apart, to separate them emotionally.

clue.text: Soldier likely to drop — almost dead — reveals pattern

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper, who drops from aircraft

indicators.note: only nearly all the word is used, so its final letter is cut

parts.note: gone means dead

explanation.surface: A collapsing soldier, nearly dead, shows the example of courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts GONE to GON. 'likely to drop' sounds like exhaustion but describes a parachutist.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a model of excellence, a pattern for others to follow.

clue.text: Quiet snow leopard to attack as cats do

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
the ounce is another name for the snow leopard

explanation.surface: A silent snow leopard springing on its prey.
explanation.definitionFit: To pounce is to spring suddenly on prey, as a cat does.

clue.text: Trickery from the French in great deal

indicators.note: the French article goes inside the other word

parts.note: sight can mean a great deal, as in a sight better
le is French for the

explanation.surface: French deception plays a part in a big business deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great deal' looks like a bargain but means 'a lot', as in 'a sight more'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight, as in sleight of hand, means dexterous trickery or cunning.

clue.text: Crime writer speaks about leading lady

indicators.note: the first word goes about, around, the other

parts.note: says means speaks
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen, is the country's leading lady

explanation.surface: A novelist of mysteries talks about the star actress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading lady' looks like a film star but is the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorothy L. Sayers wrote the Lord Peter Wimsey detective novels.

clue.text: Green part in smoke that rolls over tongue

indicators.note: rolling over flips the whole thing, so it reads backwards
the meadow word takes part in, goes into, the cigarette word

parts.note: a cig is a cigarette, a smoke
a lea is a grassy meadow, a green

explanation.surface: Smoke from a green leaf curling over the tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part in' puts the meadow inside the cigarette, and 'rolls over' turns the result, CILEAG, round. 'tongue' is a language here, not the organ of taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaelic is a language of Ireland and Scotland, and a tongue is a language.

clue.text: Find outskirts of Langley weird

parts.note: to unearth is to find by digging

indicators.note: the outskirts of a place are its edges, so only the word's first and last letters are used

explanation.surface: Something strange discovered on the edge of a town.
explanation.walkthrough: Langley is a town name; 'outskirts of' takes its outer letters L and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Unearthly means unnaturally strange, eerie, not of this world.

clue.text: Corrupt English teaching system

parts.note: to rot is to decay or become corrupt

explanation.surface: A rotten system for teaching the English language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' looks like an adjective or an anagram signal but is the verb ROT.
explanation.definitionFit: Rote is learning by mechanical repetition, a method of teaching and memorising.

clue.text: Spotted scavenger bringing money into hot area

indicators.note: the currency is brought into the two abbreviations

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, on taps
the yen is Japanese money

explanation.surface: A spotted carrion-eater earning cash in a hot region.
explanation.definitionFit: The spotted hyena is a well-known African carrion feeder, the classic scavenger.

clue.text: Limerick perhaps shortened to make an impression

indicators.note: the word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: Limerick is an Irish county

explanation.surface: A truncated comic poem trying to make its mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limerick' looks like the five-line verse form but is the Irish county.
explanation.definitionFit: To count is to matter, to carry weight or make an impression.

clue.text: Getting fine: villain at last going straight?

indicators.note: only the final letter of the preceding word is taken

parts.note: arrowing means moving in a straight line like an arrow

explanation.surface: A crook finally going straight is getting on fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going straight' looks like a reformed criminal but means flying like an arrow. 'fine' means thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrowing means becoming thinner, and fine can mean thin, as in a fine thread.
